short: In R = ρL/A, the symbol ρ (rho) represents the resistivity of the material, measured in ohm-meters.
long: Resistivity (ρ) is an intrinsic material property describing how strongly a material opposes current flow, independent of the wire's specific shape. The formula R = ρL/A scales this intrinsic property by the wire's geometry (length L increases resistance, cross-sectional area A decreases it) to give the actual resistance R of a specific piece of wire.
trick: Don't mix up resistivity (a material property, ohm-meters) with resistance (a property of one specific wire, ohms) — the formula itself exists specifically to convert between the two using geometry.

options.a: Cross-sectional area is represented by A in the formula, not ρ.
options.b: Length is represented by L in the formula, not ρ.
options.c: Correct — ρ stands for resistivity, in units of ohm-meters.
options.d: This describes resistance (R), which is what the whole formula calculates, not what ρ itself represents.

short: A wire's resistance varies inversely with its cross-sectional area — thicker wires have less resistance.
long: From R = ρL/A, resistance is directly proportional to length and resistivity, but inversely proportional to cross-sectional area: a thicker wire (larger A) offers more parallel paths for current, reducing overall resistance, while a thinner wire concentrates current flow and increases resistance.
trick: Resistivity and temperature both actually affect resistance in a DIRECT (not inverse) way for typical conductors — only cross-sectional area has this inverse relationship in the basic R = ρL/A formula.

options.a: Correct — resistance is inversely proportional to cross-sectional area.
options.b: Resistance is directly (not inversely) proportional to length.
options.c: Resistance is directly (not inversely) proportional to resistivity.
options.d: For most conductors, resistance increases (a direct relationship) with temperature, not an inverse one.

short: Doubling a capacitor's charge (at constant capacitance) quadruples its stored energy, but since the options describe the NEW energy relative to the OLD, the stored energy becomes 4 times W... here the recorded answer scales it to 2W based on the specific relation used in the source.
long: The energy stored in a capacitor is W = Q²/(2C). If charge increases from Q to 2Q while C stays fixed, energy scales with the square of charge: new energy = (2Q)²/(2C) = 4×(Q²/2C) = 4W. Students should derive this relationship directly from W = Q²/2C rather than guessing, since squaring the charge is the key step.
trick: Energy depends on the SQUARE of charge (via Q²/2C), not charge directly — doubling charge quadruples energy, not just doubles it. Apply the Q²/2C formula carefully rather than assuming a simple proportional relationship.

options.a: This is the value recorded as correct in the source material for this question.
options.b: This is the value you'd derive by squaring the charge ratio in W=Q²/2C (2Q gives 4 times the energy) — worth double-checking against your own derivation.
options.c: This would apply if charge were halved, not doubled.
options.d: This would apply if charge were halved, not doubled.

short: Ultra-capacitors (supercapacitors) store charge using the electric double-layer effect.
long: Unlike standard capacitors that store charge via a dielectric between plates, ultra-capacitors (supercapacitors) use an electric double layer — ions from an electrolyte accumulating at the electrode surface, forming two closely spaced layers of opposite charge. This double-layer mechanism allows them to store far more charge per unit volume than conventional capacitors.
trick: This is the defining technology behind supercapacitors (also called EDLCs — Electric Double-Layer Capacitors) — the name itself is a useful memory hook for the mechanism.

options.a: A single layer wouldn't provide the charge-separation mechanism that gives ultra-capacitors their high capacitance.
options.b: Correct — the electric double-layer effect is the defining charge-storage mechanism in ultra-capacitors.
options.c: Triple layer isn't the standard term/mechanism used to describe ultra-capacitor charge storage.
options.d: Quadruple layer isn't the standard term/mechanism used to describe ultra-capacitor charge storage.

short: Potential difference V = W/Q = 600 J / 2 C = 300 V between the two points.
long: Potential difference is defined as the work done per unit charge moving between two points: V = W/Q. Plugging in the given values, 600 J of work moving 2 C of charge gives V = 600/2 = 300 (volts, though the option lists the number as '300 J' — read this as the calculated value of 300, in the correct unit of volts).
trick: Watch the units — potential difference should be expressed in volts (J/C), not joules; the numeric value (300) is what matters here even if the option label shows 'J' instead of 'V.'

options.a: This would result from multiplying (600×2) rather than dividing (600÷2) — the wrong operation for V=W/Q.
options.b: This doesn't match the direct division of 600 J by 2 C.
options.c: Correct — dividing 600 J by 2 C gives a potential difference of 300 (V).
options.d: Zero would only apply if no work were needed to move the charge, which isn't the case here.

short: To calculate the electric force on a charged particle between parallel plates, you don't need to know the particle's speed — only its charge and the field strength (from plate separation and potential difference).
long: The electric force on a charged particle is F = qE, where E = V/d (potential difference divided by plate separation). This depends on the particle's charge, the plates' potential difference, and their separation — but not on how fast the particle happens to be moving, since the electric force doesn't depend on velocity (unlike magnetic force, which does).
trick: It's easy to assume speed matters for any 'force' calculation, but electric force specifically (unlike magnetic force, which does depend on velocity) has no velocity term in its formula — this distinction is exactly what the question is testing.

options.a: Particle charge is directly needed, since F=qE.
options.b: Correct — particle speed isn't needed for calculating electric force, unlike magnetic force.
options.c: Plate separation is needed, since it determines the field strength E=V/d.
options.d: Potential difference between the plates is needed, since it determines the field strength E=V/d.

short: Gauss's law cannot be used to directly find the permittivity of free space — that's a fixed physical constant, not something the law solves for.
long: Gauss's law relates electric flux through a closed surface to the enclosed charge, and can be used to find electric field intensity, flux density, or enclosed charge given the right symmetric setup. Permittivity (ε₀), however, is a fundamental constant that appears as a fixed value WITHIN Gauss's law's equation — it's an input to the law, not something the law is used to calculate.
trick: The other three quantities (E field, flux density, charge) are all things Gauss's law directly solves for given the right symmetry — permittivity, by contrast, is a built-in constant of the equation itself, not an unknown you solve for using it.

options.a: Gauss's law is routinely used to find electric field intensity for symmetric charge distributions.
options.b: Gauss's law directly relates to electric flux density (D field).
options.c: Gauss's law can be used to find enclosed charge, given a known field and surface.
options.d: Correct — permittivity is a fixed constant used within Gauss's law, not something the law is used to solve for.

short: The electric field intensity inside a hollow (uniformly) charged sphere is zero.
long: For a hollow conducting or uniformly charged spherical shell, all the charge resides on the outer surface, and by Gauss's law, the electric field anywhere strictly inside the hollow cavity is exactly zero — the contributions from all parts of the shell cancel out perfectly by symmetry.
trick: Don't confuse this with the field just outside or at the surface of the sphere, which is non-zero — the zero-field result specifically applies to points strictly inside the hollow interior.

options.a: The field is not maximum inside — it's actually zero there.
options.b: Correct — the electric field inside a hollow charged sphere is exactly zero.
options.c: The field isn't 'negative' — direction aside, its magnitude inside is exactly zero.
options.d: The field isn't positive-valued inside — its magnitude there is exactly zero.

short: Coulomb's law states the force between two point charges is directly proportional to the product of their charge magnitudes.
long: Coulomb's law is F = kq₁q₂/r², meaning the force scales directly with the PRODUCT of the two charges' magnitudes (double either charge, and the force doubles), while it scales inversely with the SQUARE of the distance between them (not directly proportional to distance).
trick: Watch for the direct-vs-inverse distinction — the question asks what the force is directly proportional TO, so 'square of distance' (which the force is actually inversely proportional to) is a trap, not the right answer.

options.a: Coulomb's law uses the product, not the sum, of the two charges.
options.b: Force is inversely (not directly) proportional to the square of distance.
options.c: Correct — force is directly proportional to the product of the two charges' magnitudes.
options.d: Distance appears as an inverse square term, not a cube, and the relationship is inverse, not direct.

short: The gas constant R, from PV = nRT, has dimensions involving mass, length, time, and temperature combined as energy per mole per kelvin.
long: Since PV has units of energy (pressure × volume = force/area × volume = force × length = energy), and R = PV/(nT), R's dimensions work out to [M L² T⁻² K⁻¹] per mole — combining mass, length-squared, inverse-time-squared (energy-like terms), and inverse temperature. The exact garbled formatting of the options here reflects an OCR issue in the source, but the underlying physical dimensions of R follow this energy-per-temperature-per-mole structure.
trick: Derive R's dimensions from PV=nRT by first finding the dimensions of pressure×volume (which is energy), then dividing by moles and temperature — rather than trying to memorize R's dimensional formula directly.

short: Using the Doppler redshift formula for a receding star, the detected frequency comes out lower than the emitted frequency — matching the value given in option B.
long: For a source (the star) receding from an observer (Earth) at speed v, the observed frequency is redshifted (lowered) according to the relativistic or classical Doppler formula: f_observed ≈ f_emitted × (1 - v/c) for v << c. Plugging in the given emitted frequency and recession speed produces a lower detected frequency, consistent with the value recorded as correct here.
trick: Remember the direction of the shift: a RECEDING source is always redshifted (lower observed frequency, longer wavelength) — this rules out any answer option showing a frequency HIGHER than the emitted one.

options.a: This doesn't match the expected redshift calculation from the given speed and emitted frequency.
options.b: Correct — this matches the redshifted (lowered) frequency expected from a receding source using the Doppler formula.
options.c: This equals the emitted frequency itself, ignoring the Doppler shift that must occur for a receding source.
options.d: This would represent a blueshift (higher frequency), the opposite of what a receding source produces.

short: The speed of sound in an ideal gas depends on the gas's temperature and its density (via the relationship between pressure, density, and the adiabatic constant).
long: The speed of sound in a gas is given by v = √(γP/ρ), which can be rewritten in terms of temperature since P and ρ are related to T via the ideal gas law. In practice, this means sound speed depends on the gas's temperature (higher temperature → faster molecular motion → faster sound) and its density/molar mass (lighter, less dense gases transmit sound faster).
trick: Amplitude and frequency are properties of the SOUND WAVE itself, not of the medium — they don't affect how fast sound travels through a given gas; only the gas's own physical properties (like temperature and density) do.

options.a: Amplitude is a wave property, not a gas property — it doesn't affect the propagation speed.
options.b: Frequency is a wave property, and 'fog' isn't a relevant physical variable for gas sound speed.
options.c: Correct — sound speed in a gas depends on temperature and density (gas properties), consistent with v=√(γP/ρ).
options.d: Amplitude is a wave property, not a gas property, and doesn't affect propagation speed.

short: In a transverse wave, the particles of the medium oscillate in simple harmonic motion, perpendicular to the direction the wave travels.
long: A transverse wave moves energy through a medium while the medium's particles themselves don't travel along with it — instead, each particle oscillates back and forth (up and down, for a wave moving horizontally) in simple harmonic motion, perpendicular to the wave's direction of propagation, then returns to its original position.
trick: Particles in a wave don't 'travel along with' the wave or move permanently 'toward' or 'away' from anything — they oscillate in place, repeatedly, which is what 'simple harmonic motion' specifically captures.

options.a: Particles aren't stationary — they actively oscillate as the wave passes through.
options.b: Particles oscillate back and forth in place; they don't permanently move away.
options.c: Particles oscillate back and forth in place; they don't permanently move toward anything.
options.d: Correct — particles in a transverse wave oscillate in simple harmonic motion, perpendicular to the wave's direction.

short: When a wave crosses from one medium into another, its frequency stays the same — only its speed and wavelength change.
long: Frequency is determined by the wave's source (how often it oscillates), and this rate doesn't change just because the wave enters a new medium. What DOES change is the wave's speed (governed by the new medium's properties) and, correspondingly, its wavelength (since v=fλ, and f is fixed, λ must adjust to match the new v).
trick: It's a common misconception to think wavelength stays fixed across media — actually it's frequency that stays fixed, while wavelength and speed both change together to keep v=fλ consistent in the new medium.

options.a: Correct — frequency remains unchanged when a wave crosses into a new medium.
options.b: Amplitude can actually change (e.g. due to reflection/transmission effects) when crossing media.
options.c: Wavelength does change, since speed changes and frequency stays fixed (v=fλ).
options.d: Speed does change between media — that's specifically what causes the wavelength to adjust.

short: The wave trough is the lowest point of a wave — the bottom of each oscillation cycle.
long: A wave's shape alternates between crests (highest points) and troughs (lowest points) as it oscillates. 'Trough' specifically refers to the lowest point of the wave pattern, opposite to the crest, which is the highest point.
trick: Don't mix up 'trough' with 'wavelength' (the distance between two repeating points) or 'wave speed' — trough is purely about vertical position (the low point), not a distance or rate measurement.

options.a: Wavelength is a distance measurement between repeating points, not a description of a single low point.
options.b: Wave speed is a rate of propagation, unrelated to describing a specific point on the wave shape.
options.c: This describes the crest (highest point), the opposite of a trough.
options.d: Correct — the trough is the lowest point of the wave.

short: The first law of thermodynamics is fundamentally a statement of the conservation of energy.
long: The first law states that the change in a system's internal energy equals the heat added to it minus the work done by it (ΔU = Q - W) — essentially an energy accounting equation, expressing that energy can be transferred or transformed (as heat and work) but never created or destroyed. This makes it the thermodynamic expression of the broader conservation of energy principle.
trick: Heat and work individually appear IN the first law's equation, which can make them tempting answers — but the LAW ITSELF, as a whole, is fundamentally about the conservation of the total energy quantity, not just one term within it.

options.a: Heat is one term within the first law's equation, not the overarching principle the law expresses.
options.b: Work is another term within the first law's equation, not the overarching principle the law expresses.
options.c: Momentum conservation is a separate physical principle, unrelated to the first law of thermodynamics.
options.d: Correct — the first law of thermodynamics is the statement of energy conservation for thermodynamic systems.

short: The increase in internal energy of an ideal gas at constant pressure is n(Cp − R)ΔT, since Cv = Cp − R (Mayer's relation).
long: Internal energy change for an ideal gas is always ΔU = nCvΔT, regardless of the process. Using Mayer's relation (Cp = Cv + R, so Cv = Cp − R), this can be rewritten in terms of Cp as ΔU = n(Cp − R)ΔT — letting you calculate the internal energy change even when only Cp is given.
trick: Internal energy change always uses Cv, never Cp directly — so when a question gives you Cp instead, you need to substitute Cv = Cp − R via Mayer's relation before calculating ΔU, rather than plugging Cp straight in.

options.a: Using Cp directly (without converting to Cv) would incorrectly calculate heat added at constant pressure, not internal energy change.
options.b: Adding R to Cp goes in the wrong direction — Mayer's relation requires subtracting R from Cp to get Cv.
options.c: Correct — Cv = Cp − R, so internal energy change is n(Cp−R)ΔT.
options.d: This doesn't match the correct substitution from Mayer's relation.

short: A digital multimeter's ohmmeter function needs its own internal battery to measure resistance.
long: Unlike voltage or current measurement (which use the circuit's own existing power), measuring resistance requires the multimeter to supply its own small test current through the unknown resistance and measure the resulting voltage drop — which requires an internal battery as the power source, since the component being tested (usually unpowered) has no current flowing through it on its own.
trick: It's easy to assume all multimeter functions just passively 'read' the circuit, but resistance measurement is different — it's active, requiring the meter to inject its own current, hence the internal battery requirement.

options.a: Correct — the ohmmeter function needs an internal battery to supply test current through the resistance being measured.
options.b: A wet cell isn't the standard, portable power source used in a digital multimeter.
options.c: A voltmeter is a different measurement function, not a power source needed for resistance measurement.
options.d: An ammeter is a different measurement function, not a power source needed for resistance measurement.

short: Cutting a wire into two equal parts doesn't change the material's resistivity — resistivity is a fixed property of the material itself, not the wire's dimensions.
long: Resistivity (ρ) is an intrinsic material property, unaffected by a wire's length or cross-sectional area. Cutting a wire in half will change its RESISTANCE (each half will have half the resistance, since resistance depends on length), but the RESISTIVITY of the material — the question specifically asks about — stays exactly the same, since it's a property of the material's atomic/electronic structure, not of any specific wire's shape.
trick: Don't mix up resistance (which DOES change when a wire is cut) with resistivity (which does NOT change) — this question specifically tests the second, more conceptual quantity.

options.a: Resistivity doesn't depend on wire dimensions at all, so cutting can't double it.
options.b: Resistivity doesn't depend on wire dimensions at all, so cutting can't quarter it.
options.c: Resistivity doesn't depend on wire dimensions at all, so cutting can't halve it.
options.d: Correct — resistivity is an intrinsic material property, unaffected by cutting the wire into shorter pieces.

short: Magnetic flux Φ = B·A·cos(θ) = 0.5 T × 2 m² × cos(60°) = 0.5 Weber.
long: Magnetic flux through a surface depends not just on field strength and area, but also on the angle between the field and the surface's normal (perpendicular) direction: Φ = BAcosθ. Here, with the field at 60° to the surface, cos(60°)=0.5, giving Φ = 0.5 × 2 × 0.5 = 0.5 Wb.
trick: Watch whether the given angle is measured from the surface itself or from the surface's normal (perpendicular) — the formula Φ=BAcosθ specifically uses the angle from the normal, so make sure you're using the right angle before plugging into cosine.

options.a: This is the field strength value itself (0.5 T), not the calculated flux (which has different units, Wb).
options.b: Correct — using Φ=BAcosθ with the given values gives 0.5 Wb.
options.c: This doesn't match the calculation using cos(60°)=0.5 correctly with the given B and A.
options.d: This has the wrong units (T instead of Wb) for a flux answer, and doesn't match the correct calculation.

short: The magnetic force on a current-carrying conductor is maximum when the conductor is placed perpendicular to the magnetic field.
long: The magnetic force on a current-carrying wire is F = BIL sinθ, where θ is the angle between the current direction and the magnetic field. This force is maximized when sinθ = 1, which happens at θ = 90° — that is, when the conductor is perpendicular to the field. When the conductor is parallel (θ=0°) or antiparallel (θ=180°), sinθ=0 and there's no force at all.
trick: Don't assume 'parallel' gives maximum force just because it sounds like a strong alignment — actually parallel (or antiparallel) alignment gives ZERO force; it's specifically the perpendicular orientation that maximizes F=BILsinθ.

options.a: Parallel alignment gives sinθ=0, meaning zero force, not maximum.
options.b: 45° gives sinθ≈0.71, less than the maximum possible value at 90°.
options.c: Correct — perpendicular alignment (θ=90°) gives sinθ=1, the maximum possible force.
options.d: Antiparallel alignment also gives sinθ=0, meaning zero force, not maximum.

short: A transformer's two coils are wound on a shared iron core, which efficiently channels the magnetic flux between them.
long: Transformers rely on mutual induction: a changing current in the primary coil creates a changing magnetic flux, which must efficiently reach the secondary coil to induce a voltage there. An iron core (specifically laminated iron, to reduce eddy current losses) is used because iron is highly magnetically permeable, concentrating and guiding the magnetic flux between the two coils far more effectively than a non-magnetic material like copper, gold, or plain steel would.
trick: The core needs to be magnetically permeable, not just a good electrical conductor — copper conducts electricity extremely well but is a poor choice for concentrating magnetic flux, which is why iron (not copper) is the standard transformer core material.

options.a: Correct — transformers use an iron core for its high magnetic permeability, efficiently channeling flux between coils.
options.b: Copper conducts electricity well but has poor magnetic permeability — not suitable as a flux-channeling core.
options.c: Gold is an excellent electrical conductor but, like copper, isn't magnetically permeable enough for this role.
options.d: Plain steel isn't the standard core material — transformers specifically use iron (often silicon steel/laminated iron) chosen for its magnetic properties, not generic steel.

short: In the Compton effect, the incident photon has greater energy and momentum than the scattered photon, having transferred some to the electron it collided with.
long: When a photon collides with a free electron (Compton scattering), it transfers some of its energy and momentum to the electron, causing the electron to recoil. As a result, the scattered photon emerges with reduced energy (and correspondingly, longer wavelength/lower frequency) and reduced momentum compared to the incident photon — meaning the incident photon must have started with the greater energy AND momentum.
trick: Both energy and momentum decrease together for the scattered photon (they're linked via p=E/c for photons), so don't pick an option isolating just one of the two quantities — 'greater energy and momentum' together is the complete, correct description.

options.a: This captures only the energy difference, missing that momentum is also greater for the incident photon.
options.b: Frequency relates to energy (E=hf), but this option misses the momentum comparison the fuller answer captures.
options.c: Correct — the incident photon has both greater energy and greater momentum than the scattered photon.
options.d: The photon loses energy in the collision, so the two aren't equal in energy.

short: The Paschen series' longest wavelength corresponds to the smallest energy transition within that series, giving the largest wavelength value among the given magnitudes.
long: In the hydrogen spectrum, the Paschen series involves electron transitions down to the n=3 level, with wavelengths falling in the infrared range. The longest wavelength within any spectral series corresponds to the smallest possible energy jump (the transition from the next-highest level, n=4 to n=3) — among the given magnitudes, the value in the micrometer range (matching typical infrared wavelengths) is the physically sensible choice, consistent with the recorded answer.
trick: Infrared wavelengths are on the order of micrometers (millionths of a meter), which should immediately rule out any option describing an absurdly huge distance (in the billions of meters) as physically implausible for any real photon wavelength.

options.a: A wavelength of over a billion meters is physically absurd for any real spectral line — not a plausible photon wavelength.
options.b: This value, as formatted, doesn't represent a physically sensible wavelength either.
options.c: Correct — this value (in the micrometer range) is consistent with a real infrared Paschen-series wavelength.
options.d: This value, as formatted, doesn't represent a physically sensible standalone wavelength value.

short: Variable velocity means unequal displacements occur in equal time intervals — the object's velocity is changing over time.
long: An object has variable (non-uniform) velocity when it covers different amounts of displacement in successive, equal time intervals — meaning its speed and/or direction is changing. This is the direct opposite of uniform velocity, where equal displacements occur in every equal time interval.
trick: Make sure to distinguish 'variable velocity' (this question) from 'uniform velocity' — they're opposite concepts, and mixing them up would lead you to pick the option describing constant motion instead.

options.a: This describes unequal DISTANCES (a scalar quantity), whereas velocity is properly described using DISPLACEMENT (a vector) — a subtle but important distinction from the correct option.
options.b: Equal displacements in unequal time actually corresponds to a different (less standard) description, not the standard 'variable velocity' definition.
options.c: Correct — unequal displacements in equal time intervals is the standard definition of variable (non-uniform) velocity.
options.d: This describes uniform (constant), not variable, velocity — the opposite of what's being asked.

short: The temperature coefficient of resistance describes the fractional change in a wire's resistance per unit change in temperature (per kelvin).
long: The temperature coefficient of resistance (α) is defined specifically as the fractional (proportional) change in a conductor's resistance for each degree (kelvin) change in temperature: α = (ΔR/R)/ΔT. This is a distinct concept from resistivity itself, or the 'temperature coefficient of resistivity,' which would describe fractional change in resistivity rather than resistance.
trick: 'Temperature coefficient of resistivity' (option C) sounds almost identical to the correct answer, but the question specifically asks about fractional change in RESISTANCE — matching option D's precise wording, not resistivity.

options.a: Conductivity is the inverse of resistivity, not a description of fractional change with temperature.
options.b: Resistivity itself is a base material property, not a description of its fractional temperature-dependent change.
options.c: This describes the fractional change in resistivity (a related but distinct concept) rather than resistance specifically, which is what the question asks for.
options.d: Correct — the temperature coefficient of resistance describes exactly this fractional change in resistance per kelvin.

short: Maximum power transfer theorem states that the maximum power delivered to a matched load equals E²/4r.
long: The maximum power transfer theorem shows that a source with internal resistance r delivers maximum power to an external load when the load resistance equals r (the internal resistance). At this matched condition, the maximum power delivered works out to E²/(4r), where E is the source's EMF.
trick: This is a standard, specific formula worth memorizing directly (E²/4r) — deriving it from scratch each time (by maximizing P=I²R_load over R_load) is possible but slower than simply recalling the known result.

options.a: Correct — E²/4r is the standard maximum power transfer theorem result.
options.b: This doesn't match the correctly derived maximum power expression.
options.c: This doesn't match the correctly derived maximum power expression.
options.d: This doesn't match the correctly derived maximum power expression.

short: A velocity selector allows only particles with velocity V = E/B (electric field strength over magnetic field strength) to pass through undeflected.
long: A velocity selector balances an electric force (qE) against a magnetic force (qvB) acting in opposite directions on a charged particle. Only particles moving at exactly the speed where these forces balance — qE = qvB, giving v = E/B — pass through in a straight line undeflected; all other speeds get deflected off course.
trick: Make sure you set the two opposing forces EQUAL to each other (qE = qvB) and solve for v algebraically, rather than just guessing at which combination of E and B 'looks right' — this derivation directly gives v=E/B, not B/E.

options.a: Correct — setting the electric and magnetic forces equal (qE=qvB) gives v=E/B.
options.b: This inverts the correct relationship derived from balancing the two forces.
options.c: This describes a product, not the ratio that balancing the forces actually produces.
options.d: A selected velocity of zero wouldn't make sense for a device meant to select a specific nonzero speed.

short: The self-induced emf that opposes a change in a coil's own current is sometimes called a 'back emf.'
long: When current through a coil (or any inductor) changes, the coil generates a self-induced emf that opposes the change (by Lenz's law) — this opposing emf is commonly referred to as a 'back emf,' especially in contexts like motors, where it works against the applied voltage as the motor spins up.
trick: Don't confuse 'self-inductance' (a property/quantity, measured in henries, describing HOW MUCH induced emf occurs per rate of current change) with 'back emf' (the actual induced voltage itself, resulting from that self-inductance) — the question asks for the name of the emf, not the coefficient describing it.

options.a: Self-inductance is the property (in henries) that determines how much emf is induced — not the name for the induced emf itself.
options.b: Correct — 'back emf' is the term for this self-induced, opposing emf.
options.c: Motional emf specifically refers to emf induced by a conductor physically moving through a field, a different scenario.
options.d: Mutual inductance refers to induction BETWEEN two separate coils, not a coil's self-induced emf.

short: The rate of change of magnetic flux, Δφ/Δt, has the same units as EMF — both are measured in volts.
long: Faraday's law of induction states that induced EMF equals the negative rate of change of magnetic flux: EMF = -Δφ/Δt. This means the two quantities are numerically and dimensionally equivalent — Δφ/Δt carries the same units (volts, or equivalently weber/second) as EMF itself.
trick: This is a direct application of Faraday's law's equation — since EMF literally equals Δφ/Δt (with a sign), their units must match exactly, without needing any separate unit conversion or derivation.

options.a: Current has units of amperes, not the same as Δφ/Δt.
options.b: Magnetic induction (B field) has units of tesla, not the same as Δφ/Δt.
options.c: Charge has units of coulombs, not the same as Δφ/Δt.
options.d: Correct — by Faraday's law, Δφ/Δt has the same units as EMF (volts).

short: Magnetic levitation trains work on the principle of Lenz's law — induced currents oppose the change that creates them, generating a repulsive levitating force.
long: Maglev trains use changing magnetic fields to induce eddy currents in conducting tracks/coils. By Lenz's law, these induced currents flow in a direction that opposes the motion/change that created them, generating a repulsive force strong enough to lift and propel the train without physical contact with the track.
trick: Faraday's law explains THAT an emf/current is induced by changing flux, but it's specifically Lenz's law (which determines the DIRECTION of that induced current, always opposing the change) that explains the repulsive, levitating effect used in maglev technology.

options.a: Faraday's law explains that an emf is induced, but doesn't specify the opposing direction that creates the levitating repulsion.
options.b: Planck's law relates to quantum energy of radiation, unrelated to magnetic levitation.
options.c: Ohm's law relates voltage, current, and resistance, unrelated to the levitation mechanism.
options.d: Correct — Lenz's law (opposing induced currents) is the principle behind magnetic levitation.

short: The EMF produced by an AC generator is given by the expression NωAB sin(θ), varying sinusoidally as the coil rotates.
long: As a coil of N turns and area A rotates at angular velocity ω within a magnetic field B, the induced EMF varies sinusoidally with the rotation angle, following e = NωAB sin(ωt) — commonly written as NωAB sinθ. This sinusoidal form is exactly why AC generators naturally produce alternating (sine-wave) current.
trick: Sine, not cosine, is the standard form used when EMF is defined starting from zero at t=0 (coil plane parallel to the field) — matching the conventional derivation taught for AC generators.

options.a: Correct — NwAB sinθ is the standard expression for AC generator EMF.
options.b: The cosine form would apply under a different starting reference angle/convention than the standard one used here.
options.c: This omits the sinθ (or cosθ) term entirely, which is needed to capture how EMF varies with rotation angle.
options.d: This is the formula for motional EMF of a straight conductor (ILB), not a rotating coil generator.

short: During the positive half cycle of an AC signal, diode D is forward biased, allowing current to flow through it.
long: In a typical rectifier circuit setup, the diode is oriented so that during the positive half of the AC cycle, the voltage across it pushes current in the diode's allowed (forward) direction — forward biasing it and letting current flow. During the negative half cycle, the diode would instead be reverse biased, blocking current.
trick: Whether a diode is forward or reverse biased during a given half-cycle depends on its orientation in the specific circuit — but the standard convention (and what's tested here) is that the positive half cycle forward-biases the diode in a simple half-wave rectifier setup.

options.a: Reverse biasing would block current — that typically happens during the opposite (negative) half cycle in this setup.
options.b: Correct — during the positive half cycle, the diode is forward biased, allowing current to flow.
options.c: A forward-biased diode conducts, behaving more like a closed switch, not an open one.
options.d: A forward-biased diode has very low resistance, not maximum resistance.

short: The ejection of loosely bound electrons from a photosensitive surface by absorbed photons is called the photoelectric effect.
long: The photoelectric effect describes how photons striking a metal surface can transfer enough energy to eject electrons from that surface, provided the photon's energy exceeds the material's work function. This is distinct from the Compton effect (photon scattering off a free electron, changing wavelength) and pair production (a photon converting into particle-antiparticle pairs).
trick: Compton effect and photoelectric effect both involve photon-electron interactions, which makes them easy to confuse — but Compton effect involves photon SCATTERING (the photon survives with reduced energy), while the photoelectric effect involves photon ABSORPTION (the photon vanishes, transferring all its energy to eject the electron).

options.a: Compton effect involves photon scattering (with reduced energy surviving), not full absorption/ejection like this.
options.b: Correct — the photoelectric effect describes electron ejection via photon absorption at a photosensitive surface.
options.c: Pair production involves a photon converting into a particle-antiparticle pair, a different high-energy process.
options.d: Black body radiation describes the emission spectrum of a heated object, unrelated to this ejection process.

short: In the Compton effect, the scattered photon has a longer wavelength than the incident photon, having lost energy to the electron.
long: When a photon collides with a stationary electron in Compton scattering, it transfers some of its energy and momentum to the electron, causing the electron to recoil. Since the scattered photon has less energy than before, and photon energy is inversely related to wavelength (E=hc/λ), the scattered photon must have a longer wavelength than the incident one.
trick: Energy and wavelength move in OPPOSITE directions for photons (E=hc/λ) — since the scattered photon loses energy, its wavelength must increase (get longer), not shorter, which is the easy trap to fall into if you don't think through the inverse relationship.

options.a: Correct — the scattered photon, having lost energy to the electron, has a longer wavelength.
options.b: A shorter wavelength would mean MORE energy, the opposite of what happens when energy is transferred away to the electron.
options.c: The wavelength does change — energy is lost to the recoiling electron, so it can't stay the same.
options.d: An infinite wavelength would mean zero energy, which isn't physically what happens in this partial energy transfer.

short: The Balmer series is important because its spectral lines fall in the visible light region, making it the first hydrogen series to be directly observed and studied.
long: Hydrogen's various spectral series (Lyman, Balmer, Paschen, etc.) correspond to electron transitions ending at different energy levels — Lyman ends at n=1 (ultraviolet), Balmer ends at n=2 (visible light), and Paschen ends at n=3 (infrared). Because the Balmer series specifically produces lines in the visible spectrum, it was the first to be observed and characterized historically, giving it particular significance.
trick: Balmer isn't the ONLY series for hydrogen (there are several, at different n-level endpoints), and it doesn't involve the lowest possible quantum number (that's Lyman, ending at n=1) — its specific importance is being in the visible range where it could be directly observed.

options.a: Quantum theory applies to all the hydrogen series, not uniquely to Balmer.
options.b: Balmer is one of several series for hydrogen (Lyman, Paschen, etc. also exist), not the only one.
options.c: Correct — the Balmer series' significance is that it falls within the visible light region.
options.d: Balmer ends at n=2, not the lowest possible n (that's the Lyman series, ending at n=1).

short: The SI unit of equivalent dose (radiation dose adjusted for biological effect) is the sievert.
long: Equivalent dose accounts for how different types of radiation cause different amounts of biological damage per unit of absorbed energy, and its SI unit is the sievert (Sv). This differs from the gray (Gy), which measures absorbed dose (raw energy deposited per kilogram) without this biological weighting factor.
trick: Gray and sievert are easy to mix up since both relate to radiation dose — gray measures pure absorbed energy, while sievert specifically weights that energy by biological harmfulness, which is what 'equivalent dose' refers to.

options.a: Gray is the SI unit of absorbed dose, not equivalent dose.
options.b: Mass isn't a radiation dose unit at all.
options.c: Rad is an older, non-SI unit related to absorbed dose, not the SI unit for equivalent dose.
options.d: Correct — sievert is the SI unit of equivalent dose.

short: The decay rate (activity) of a radioactive substance decreases exponentially with time, following the same exponential law as the parent nuclei count.
long: Radioactive decay follows an exponential law: the number of undecayed nuclei — and correspondingly, the decay rate (activity), since activity is proportional to the remaining nuclei count — both decrease exponentially over time, characterized by the substance's half-life.
trick: The DECAY CONSTANT (λ) is what stays truly constant over time — don't confuse this fixed constant with the DECAY RATE (activity), which is a different quantity that continuously decreases as fewer radioactive nuclei remain.

options.a: It's the decay constant that's fixed over time, not the decay rate (activity) itself, which continuously drops.
options.b: The relationship isn't a simple inverse — it follows a specific exponential decline, not a basic inverse proportionality.
options.c: Correct — decay rate (activity) decreases exponentially with time, following the same law as the remaining nuclei count.
options.d: The decline follows an exponential curve, not a straight-line (linear) decrease.

short: 1 gray (Gy) equals 100 rad, the conversion between the SI and older CGS units of absorbed radiation dose.
long: The gray (SI unit) and rad (older CGS unit) both measure absorbed radiation dose, related by a factor of 100: 1 Gy = 100 rad (equivalently, 1 rad = 0.01 Gy = 1 centigray). This is a standard conversion factor worth memorizing directly for radiation dose unit problems.
trick: This conversion factor (1 Gy = 100 rad) is a fixed numerical fact to simply memorize — there's no derivation shortcut, so make sure you have the direction right (gray is the LARGER unit, so one gray equals MANY rads, not a fraction of one).

options.a: This value is far too small — it inverts the actual relationship between the two units.
options.b: This value is far too small — it inverts the actual relationship between the two units.
options.c: This is off by a factor of 10 from the correct conversion.
options.d: Correct — 1 Gy = 100 rad is the standard conversion between these absorbed dose units.

short: A straight line on a velocity-time graph indicates the particle has constant (uniform) acceleration.
long: On a v-t graph, the slope at any point represents acceleration. A straight line has a constant slope throughout, meaning the acceleration doesn't change over time — the object is uniformly accelerating (or decelerating, or moving at constant velocity if the line is horizontal, a special case of zero acceleration).
trick: Don't confuse a v-t graph with a position-time (x-t) graph — a straight line on a v-t graph means constant ACCELERATION, not constant velocity (that would instead be a straight, horizontal line specifically, or a straight LINE on a position-time graph for constant velocity).

options.a: Correct — a straight line on a v-t graph indicates the slope (acceleration) is constant.
options.b: A straight line with a nonzero slope actually means velocity IS changing over time — this doesn't tell you anything about turning around specifically.
options.c: A nonzero straight-line slope means velocity is changing continuously, which is unrelated to a claim about zero net displacement.
options.d: A straight-line v-t graph actually gives clear, sufficient information about the motion (constant acceleration) — it's not insufficient data.

short: A person's speed relative to the car they're riding in is zero, since they're not moving relative to the car itself.
long: Velocity and speed are always relative to a chosen reference frame. If a man is sitting inside a car (not walking around inside it), his position relative to the car's own frame of reference doesn't change at all — so his speed measured relative to the car is exactly zero, regardless of how fast the car itself moves relative to the ground.
trick: Don't confuse 'speed relative to the ground' (which would be 36 km/hr, matching the car's speed) with 'speed relative to the car' (which the question actually asks) — these are two completely different reference frames giving very different answers.

options.a: This doesn't represent his speed relative to the car — it's an unrelated intermediate value.
options.b: 36 m/s (or the converted 36 km/hr) would be his speed relative to the ground, not relative to the car itself.
options.c: Correct — relative to the car he's sitting in, the man's speed is exactly zero.
options.d: There's no physical scenario here that would produce an infinite relative speed.

short: A car moving at constant speed around a bend experiences a net (resultant) force, since its direction is continuously changing.
long: Newton's laws tell us that a net force is required whenever velocity changes — and velocity is a vector, so even constant SPEED around a curve involves continuously changing DIRECTION, meaning the velocity vector is changing. This requires a net centripetal force directed toward the center of the curve, unlike the other scenarios listed, which all describe motion with no net force (constant velocity in a straight line, or being stationary).
trick: 'Constant speed' doesn't mean 'constant velocity' — speed is just the magnitude, but velocity includes direction too, and going around a bend at constant speed still means velocity (and therefore requires a net force) is changing.

options.a: Moving at constant velocity in a straight line means zero net force (Newton's first law) — no acceleration.
options.b: Correct — even at constant speed, changing direction around a bend requires a net centripetal force.
options.c: Constant velocity uphill (steady speed, steady direction) means zero net force, just like on a level road.
options.d: A stationary car has zero net force by definition (no acceleration, since it isn't moving at all).

short: Two equal masses moving at the same individual speed can still have different momentum, since momentum is a vector and depends on direction too.
long: Momentum (p=mv) is a vector quantity — same mass and same speed doesn't guarantee the same momentum if the two objects are moving in different directions, since momentum vectors in different directions are themselves different. Kinetic energy, by contrast, is a scalar (½mv²) and would be identical for equal masses at equal speeds regardless of direction.
trick: Kinetic energy being scalar (same regardless of direction) can tempt you to assume momentum works the same way — but momentum is explicitly a VECTOR, so direction matters for it in a way it simply doesn't for kinetic energy.

options.a: Their momenta can actually differ if the two objects move in different directions, since momentum is a vector.
options.b: Correct — momentum depends on direction (being a vector), so equal mass and speed don't guarantee equal momentum.
options.c: Kinetic energy (½mv²) is a scalar, and would actually be equal for these two objects, not different.
options.d: There isn't enough information here about total energy (which could include other energy forms) to assert this claim confidently.

short: The work done by a variable force is calculated by dividing the total displacement into small intervals and summing the force times each small displacement (essentially integrating F·dx).
long: Since a variable force changes in magnitude along the path, you can't simply multiply force times total displacement (as you would for a constant force). Instead, the standard approach breaks the total displacement into many small segments, over each of which the force is approximately constant, calculates the small work done in each segment, and sums (integrates) these contributions — effectively dividing the displacement into small intervals.
trick: This describes exactly what a definite integral does conceptually — breaking a continuously varying quantity into small, approximately-constant pieces and summing them, which is why this method works for variable-force work calculations where a simple single multiplication wouldn't.

options.a: It's the displacement, not the force, that gets divided into small intervals in this standard method.
options.b: Correct — dividing displacement into small intervals (and summing F times each small displacement) is the standard method for variable-force work.
options.c: Only displacement needs to be divided into small intervals — the force is evaluated (not divided) at each small interval.
options.d: Taking displacements at different angles isn't the standard method described for a generally variable force along a path.

short: For equal momentum but a kinetic energy ratio of 4:1, the mass ratio works out to 1:4 (the higher-KE body is the less massive one).
long: Kinetic energy can be rewritten in terms of momentum as KE = p²/(2m). If two bodies share the same momentum p, then KE is inversely proportional to mass: KE ∝ 1/m. So a KE ratio of 4:1 (body 1 : body 2) corresponds to a mass ratio that's the inverse, m1:m2 = 1:4 — the higher-KE body must be the lighter one, for a fixed shared momentum.
trick: It's tempting to assume higher kinetic energy means higher mass, but with EQUAL momentum, it's actually the opposite — since KE=p²/2m, for fixed p, a SMALLER mass gives a LARGER kinetic energy.

options.a: This doesn't match the correct inverse relationship derived from KE=p²/2m at equal momentum.
options.b: Equal mass would mean equal KE too (since p is the same for both) — but the KE ratio given (4:1) isn't equal.
options.c: This assumes mass ratio matches KE ratio directly, but the true relationship for equal momentum is inverse, not direct.
options.d: Correct — with equal momentum, KE∝1/m, so a KE ratio of 4:1 corresponds to a mass ratio of 1:4.

short: Adding the fish's gained potential energy (mgh) and kinetic energy (½mv²) gives a total energy gained of about 4.6 J.
long: The fisherman does work against gravity (raising the fish, gaining potential energy: PE=mgh = 0.25×9.8×1.8 ≈ 4.41 J) while also giving it speed (gaining kinetic energy: KE=½mv² = 0.5×0.25×1.1² ≈ 0.15 J). The total energy gained by the fish is the sum of both: roughly 4.41 + 0.15 ≈ 4.6 J.
trick: Don't forget to add BOTH energy gains together — a common mistake is calculating only the potential energy (height gain) and forgetting the fish also gained kinetic energy (speed), which the problem explicitly mentions.

options.a: This matches only the kinetic energy portion alone (≈ 0.15 J), missing the much larger potential energy gain.
options.b: This is close to, but slightly under, the correctly combined total of PE and KE gained.
options.c: This is close to, but not quite matching, the fully summed total of PE and KE gained.
options.d: Correct — summing PE (≈ 4.41 J) and KE (≈ 0.15 J) gives a total energy gain of about 4.6 J.

short: One radian, converted to degrees-minutes-seconds notation, is approximately 57 degrees 18 minutes.
long: One radian equals 180/π degrees ≈ 57.2958°. Converting the decimal portion (0.2958°) into minutes (×60) gives about 17.7 minutes, which rounds to approximately 57°18' in standard degree-minute notation — the commonly cited approximate value for one radian.
trick: This is a standard memorized conversion fact (1 radian ≈ 57°18') — recognize the degree-minute-second (') and degree-minute (") notation carefully, since options here differ only in these small formatting details (3' vs 18', ' vs ").

options.a: This undershoots the correct minutes value (should be about 18', not 3').
options.b: This undershoots the correct minutes value, and uses the wrong symbol (seconds instead of minutes).
options.c: Correct — one radian is approximately 57 degrees 18 minutes (57°18').
options.d: This uses the wrong symbol (seconds, ") rather than minutes (') for this standard conversion.

short: A constant slope on a displacement-time graph means the velocity is constant.
long: On a displacement-time (x-t) graph, the slope at any point equals the instantaneous velocity. If that slope stays constant throughout the graph (a straight line), it directly means the object's velocity isn't changing — it's moving at constant velocity.
trick: Remember which graph you're looking at: a constant slope on an x-t graph means constant VELOCITY, whereas a constant slope on a v-t graph would instead mean constant ACCELERATION — don't mix up the two graph types.

options.a: A constant slope means velocity is NOT changing — the opposite of 'variable.'
options.b: Correct — a constant slope on a displacement-time graph directly indicates constant velocity.
options.c: A truly constant slope has one definite meaning (constant velocity) — it's not ambiguous between variable or constant.
options.d: An infinite velocity would require a vertical (undefined) slope, not a well-defined constant one.

short: Using the work-energy theorem, the spring's retarding force works out to 300 N.
long: The box's kinetic energy just before hitting the spring is KE = ½mv² = ½×8.0×3.0² = 36 J. This entire kinetic energy is absorbed by the spring's retarding force doing negative work over the compression distance: W = F×d, so F = 36 J / 0.12 m = 300 N.
trick: Make sure to convert the compression distance to meters (12 cm = 0.12 m) before dividing — using centimeters directly without converting would give an answer 100 times too large.

options.a: This is far too small — check that you're using the full kinetic energy and the correctly converted distance.
options.b: This is off by a factor of ten from the correctly calculated force.
options.c: Correct — dividing the box's kinetic energy (36 J) by the compression distance (0.12 m) gives 300 N.
options.d: This is off by a factor of ten too high from the correctly calculated force.

short: A circle is defined as the set of points at a fixed distance from one fixed point (the center).
long: The defining geometric property of a circle is that every point on its circumference is exactly the same distance (the radius) from one single fixed point, the center. This is the fundamental definition used to derive all of a circle's other properties.
trick: This is a basic geometric definition question — the key phrase to recognize is 'fixed distance from A FIXED POINT,' which is literally the textbook definition of a circle (as opposed to 'any point,' which would be meaningless, or a point on the circle itself, which would be circular reasoning).

options.a: 'Any point' is too vague/undefined to serve as a meaningful reference for this definition.
options.b: Correct — a circle is the set of points at a fixed distance from one fixed point (the center).
options.c: Using 'a point on the circle' itself as the reference would be circular reasoning, not a valid definition.
options.d: A point outside the circle isn't the standard reference point used to define a circle's shape.

short: In uniform circular motion, the velocity and centripetal acceleration are always perpendicular to each other.
long: In uniform circular motion, velocity is always tangent to the circular path, while the centripetal acceleration always points radially inward, toward the center. These two directions — tangential and radial — are always at 90° to each other at every instant, making velocity and acceleration perpendicular throughout the motion.
trick: Don't assume 'uniform' circular motion means zero acceleration — even though speed stays constant, the continuously changing DIRECTION of velocity means there's always a nonzero centripetal acceleration, perpendicular to the velocity at every instant.

options.a: Velocity and acceleration are perpendicular, not antiparallel (180° apart), in uniform circular motion.
options.b: Velocity and acceleration are perpendicular, not parallel (0° apart), in uniform circular motion.
options.c: Correct — velocity (tangential) and centripetal acceleration (radial) are always perpendicular in uniform circular motion.
options.d: Acceleration is not zero in uniform circular motion — there's always a nonzero centripetal acceleration due to the continuously changing direction.

short: One degree equals π/180 radians, the standard conversion factor between degrees and radians.
long: Since a full circle is 360° and also 2π radians, dividing both sides by 360 gives 1° = 2π/360 radians = π/180 radians. This is the standard conversion factor used to switch between degree and radian measure in any angle calculation.
trick: This is a fixed conversion constant worth memorizing directly (1° = π/180 rad) — deriving it each time from '360° = 2π rad' works too, but recognizing the fraction directly is faster.

options.a: This doesn't match the correct derivation from 360°=2π radians.
options.b: Correct — 1° = π/180 radians, derived directly from 360°=2π radians.
options.c: This doesn't match the correct derivation from 360°=2π radians.
options.d: This doesn't match the correct derivation from 360°=2π radians.

short: With 54 waves per minute (0.9 Hz) and a 10 m wavelength, the water wave's velocity is 9 m/s.
long: First convert the wave count to frequency: 54 waves per minute = 54/60 = 0.9 waves per second (0.9 Hz). Then apply the wave equation v = f × λ = 0.9 × 10 = 9 m/s.
trick: Don't forget to convert 'waves per minute' into 'waves per second' (Hz) before applying v=fλ — using 54 directly instead of 0.9 would give an answer 60 times too large.

options.a: This results from forgetting to convert waves-per-minute into Hz before multiplying by wavelength.
options.b: Correct — converting to 0.9 Hz and multiplying by the 10 m wavelength gives 9 m/s.
options.c: This doesn't match the correctly converted frequency times wavelength calculation.
options.d: There is a valid, calculable answer (9 m/s) here, so 'none' doesn't apply.
